html:
The hesychast controversy was a dispute in the Byzantine Empire, from about 1337 to 1351, over a way of prayer practised by the monks of Mount Athos. It ended with the teaching of Gregory Palamas being made part of Orthodox doctrine.

Hesychasm, from the Greek for "stillness", was a practice of quiet inner prayer. Monks sat with head bowed, controlled their breathing and repeated the Jesus Prayer, and some said they saw a divine light. Barlaam of Calabria, a learned Greek monk from southern Italy, attacked them as ignorant and mocked them as "navel-souls".

Palamas defended them by setting God's essence, which no one can know, apart from his energies, which people can experience, such as the light seen at the Transfiguration. A council in Constantinople in 1341 backed Palamas, and Barlaam went back to Italy. The quarrel then got mixed up with the civil war, since John Kantakouzenos backed the Palamites. Councils in 1347 and 1351 confirmed their victory, which still shapes Orthodox spiritual life.
sum: The hesychast controversy was a dispute in the Byzantine Empire, from about 1337 to 1351, over a way of prayer practised by the monks of Mount Athos. It ended with the teaching of Gregory Palamas being made part of Orthodox doctrine.
